tldr: The authors introduce "TAPVid-MV," a new benchmark for long-term tracking of arbitrary physical surface points in a consistent 3D world coordinate system from moving multi-camera videos, and evaluate over 30 state-of-the-art methods. The results show that existing methods fall far short of practical utility, with failures in 3D geometry recovery serving as the primary bottleneck.
hero_caption: Overview of the seven subsets comprising TAPVid-MV. Across diverse environments—robotics manipulation, sports, human contact, desktop clearing, autonomous driving, and synthetic procedural scenes—identical 3D trajectories are projected and verified across independently moving cameras.
overview:
Multi-camera systems, such as robot wrist-mounted views combined with external static cameras, are expected to provide robustness against occlusions and reduce depth ambiguity. However, existing point-tracking benchmarks are limited to single videos or static rigs, lacking a unified dataset to measure whether a point specified in a single camera can be tracked long-term in a 3D world coordinate system under moving multi-view setups. It has also been impossible to separate whether 3D tracking failures stem from point correspondence errors or geometry errors in depth and camera poses.

To address this, the authors built "TAPVid-MV," the first large-scale multi-view 3D point tracking benchmark spanning 7 domains, 284 sequences, and 1,142 camera streams from robotics to autonomous driving. Leveraging domain-specific physical ground truth such as robot kinematics, LiDAR, and fitted meshes, it contains over 100,000 visually verified, high-accuracy 3D tracks. The task is to track a single surface point—specified by one query pixel in a single frame of a single camera—across all cameras and timesteps within a shared 3D world coordinate system.

Evaluating over 30 state-of-the-art baselines revealed surprising findings. Currently, no method comes close to solving this task, and trackers designed specifically for multi-view settings frequently fail to outperform monocular trackers. By decoupling and evaluating reconstruction and point tracking on the same data, the authors found that the primary obstacle is multi-view dynamic scene geometry recovery. Merely improving geometry quality can double tracking accuracy, pointing to a clear roadmap for future 3D dynamic perception research.
contributions: Introduced "TAPVid-MV," the first benchmark for tracking 3D point trajectories in a shared world coordinate system from a single query pixel across multiple moving cameras.
Designed a three-stage evaluation framework across query view (Q), non-query views (N), and world space (W) to disentangle point correspondence errors from geometric reconstruction errors.

Extensively evaluated over 30 state-of-the-art baselines (2D/3D, monocular/multi-view, modular/end-to-end) under uniform conditions, revealing severe limitations of existing approaches in practical scenarios.
Identified dynamic multi-view geometry recovery (depth and camera pose) as the main bottleneck hindering tracking accuracy, establishing key priorities for future improvement.
Publicly released the procedural generator "Perpetua" and high-precision 3D trajectory annotations for 5,371 episodes of the DROID robot manipulation dataset for the research community.

sections.heading: Why can't we track 3D points despite having multiple cameras?
sections.summary: While multiple viewpoints should resolve monocular depth ambiguity and overcome occlusions, existing benchmarks have focused on single videos or static cameras. This paper introduces "TAPVid-MV," the first large-scale benchmark designed to evaluate long-term 3D point tracking in dynamic scenes with camera motion.
sections.details:
Multi-camera systems have become commonplace in robotics, autonomous driving, and AR/VR. With multiple perspectives, points occluded in one view can remain visible from another, providing absolute depth cues that are difficult to infer from monocular video. However, prior benchmarks measuring 3D point tracking (TAP-3D) performance have been restricted to monocular video or fixed static camera rigs. No benchmark evaluated realistic multi-camera setups where the cameras themselves move independently.

Complicating matters further, the root causes of 3D tracking errors often remain a black box. Modern methods typically either lift 2D tracks to 3D using estimated depth, track directly within a reconstructed 3D space, or perform end-to-end joint geometry and tracking. Consequently, when tracking fails, it has been impossible to determine whether the culprit was 2D correspondence matching or depth and camera pose geometry estimation.

To bridge this gap, this paper introduces TAPVid-MV. Curated from seven indoor and outdoor domains, it spans 284 sequences, 1,142 moving camera streams, and 109,769 rigorously verified 3D trajectories. Evaluating over 30 baselines revealed that no current method comes close to solving the task, dedicated multi-view trackers fail to outperform monocular baselines, and low geometry recovery accuracy serves as the primary bottleneck for tracking.

sections.heading: From 2D to 3D, and the missing gap in multi-view tracking
sections.summary: Tracking Any Point (TAP) evolved from monocular 2D to monocular 3D, but multi-view evaluations remained limited to static rigs or required multiple queries. TAPVid-MV is the first benchmark simultaneously featuring real-world data, independent camera motion, and multi-view setups.
sections.details:
Tracking arbitrary physical surface points across entire video sequences was formalized as "Tracking Any Point (TAP)," spurring numerous high-performance 2D trackers such as CoTracker and TAPIR. This was subsequently expanded to metric 3D point trajectory tracking in monocular video via "TAP-3D."

Recently, 3D tracking combined with depth estimation models as well as 4D foundation models solving dynamic scene geometry and tracking simultaneously (e.g., SpatialTracker, OmniX) have emerged. Multi-view methods like MV-TAP and MVTracker were also proposed. However, prior multi-view evaluations suffered from major limitations. For instance, MV-TAP requires query pixels in every camera (evaluated in 2D only), while MVTracker and LAPA evaluate on static camera rigs.

In real-world robotics, arm-mounted wrist cameras move dynamically while external monitoring cameras also shift or move independently. TAPVid-MV is the first benchmark in the world to satisfy all criteria: real-world video, three or more views, moving cameras, and independently moving non-rigid setups, designed to evaluate both point tracking and 3D reconstruction concurrently on identical data.

sections.heading: Task design and metrics: Pinpointing failure modes across three coordinate spaces
sections.summary: Inputs consist solely of multi-view video streams and a single query point in one frame of one camera. Tracking is evaluated across three stages—Query View (Q), Non-Query Views (N), and World Space (W)—to isolate cross-view correspondence failures from global alignment drift.
sections.details:
The task input consists of time-synchronized RGB video streams from $V$ cameras and a set of query points. Crucially, each query $q_p=(x_p, y_p, t_p, v_p)$ is provided as a single 2D pixel coordinate in frame $t_p$ of a single query camera $v_p$. No ground-truth correspondences in other cameras are provided. This reflects practical scenarios, such as an operator clicking an object surface once to guide a robot.

The model must predict the 3D trajectory $\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{p,t}$ of that physical point across all frames in a single, shared world coordinate system. Since ground-truth camera poses and metric depth are not provided to the model, predictions are aligned via a similarity transformation (Sim(3)) before evaluation.

Extending the 3D position accuracy metric $\delta^{3D}$ (the fraction of points within distance thresholds) from TAP-3D, evaluation is broken down into three distinct spaces:

- ### Query View (Q)
Evaluates trajectories in the coordinate frame of the camera where the query was placed. This reflects standard monocular TAP-3D conditions, measuring the baseline monocular tracking capability of the model.

- ### Non-Query Views (N)
Evaluates trajectories projected into other camera coordinate frames where no query was placed. This assesses whether a point tracked in one camera is accurately associated from a vastly different perspective.

- ### World Space (W)
Evaluates trajectories in the global 3D world coordinate system shared by all cameras. Even if tracking is accurate within individual camera frames, cross-camera pose misalignment or scale drift will significantly degrade this score.

By comparing $\delta_{\mathrm{Q}}^{3D}$, $\delta_{\mathrm{N}}^{3D}$, and $\delta_{\mathrm{W}}^{3D}$, it becomes immediately clear whether a tracker failed due to monocular tracking, cross-view correspondence, or global geometric misalignment.

sections.heading: Seven domains and 100k tracks: Building rigorous ground truth
sections.summary: The benchmark includes seven subsets spanning robotics, human motion, driving, and synthetic scenes, totaling 284 sequences and 1,142 camera views. Ground-truth tracks were established using robot kinematics, stereo, LiDAR, and fitted meshes, with every sequence visually verified.
sections.details:
Manually annotating metric 3D point trajectories across moving multi-camera videos is virtually impossible for human annotators. The authors selected seven datasets with strong physical and geometric ground-truth signals, applying tailored processing pipelines for each domain:

### 4.1 DROID (Robot Manipulation)
Features 7-DoF Franka robot joint states, two static stereo cameras, and one wrist-mounted camera. Reflection noise in stereo depth was cleaned, and extrinsic calibrations were optimized against CAD models. Static background points and robot surface points derived via forward kinematics were tracked across 50 curated evaluation sequences.

### 4.2 Ego-Exo4D (Sports Activities)
Captures soccer scenes using a head-mounted camera and multiple static cameras. Human skeletal mesh fits and SLAM points were filtered using VGGT depth and SAM masks to extract trajectories observable across at least three views over long horizons.

### 4.3 Harmony4D (Human-Human Interaction)
Comprises 29 sequences with two egocentric cameras and two static cameras. SMPL mesh surface points demonstrating cycle-consistent 2D tracks via TAPNext++ were retained as reliable trajectories.

### 4.4 PACE (Tabletop Manipulation)
Contains 68 sequences of tabletop clearing with a handheld trinocular camera rig. Surface points were generated from 6-DoF object poses, and camera world poses were recovered by registering static background objects.

### 4.5 Hi4D (Close Human Contact)
Covers dense human physical interactions such as handshakes and hugs. Surface points were transferred from scanned meshes onto clothed models, yielding 8-view rendered sequences.

### 4.6 Waymo (Autonomous Driving)
Features three synchronized forward-facing vehicle cameras. 3D tracks for the ego-vehicle, surrounding vehicles, and background were mapped to a shared world frame using LiDAR points and rigid bounding box motions.

### 4.7 Perpetua (Procedural Synthetic Data)
An in-house synthetic dataset simulating four animated human avatars and four moving cameras in indoor environments, providing perfect ground-truth 3D geometry.

captions.F2: Representative frames and camera configurations across the seven subsets. As seen in the camera trajectory plots below, the benchmark covers highly dynamic camera motions, from robot wrist cameras and sports head-mounted cameras to moving vehicles.

sections.heading: Benchmarking 30+ baselines: The irony of monocular methods beating multi-view models
sections.summary: Over 30 competitive baselines were benchmarked across modular (external geometry) and joint (self-contained 4D) paradigms. Global world accuracy capped out at just 22.8%, revealing that tracking performance is bottlenecked not by tracking algorithms, but by coarse geometry recovery (depth and poses).
sections.details:
Baselines were categorized into two primary paradigms based on how they acquire geometric information:

- **Group 1 (Modular Trackers)**: Consume estimated depth and camera poses from a multi-view geometry foundation model (VGGT-$\Omega$) as shared inputs. Includes 2D monocular trackers (e.g., CoTracker3), 3D monocular trackers (e.g., TAPIP3D), multi-view 2D trackers (MV-TAP), and multi-view 3D trackers (MVTracker).
- **Group 2 (Joint 4D Models)**: Perform simultaneous shape reconstruction and tracking end-to-end without external geometry inputs. Includes monocular joint methods (e.g., SpatialTrackerV2) and multi-view joint models (OmniX).

Key empirical findings include:

### Geometric Collapse in End-to-End Multi-View Models
OmniX, an end-to-end multi-view foundation model, achieved a world space accuracy $\delta_{\mathrm{W}}^{3D}$ of only 10.3 on average, plummeting to 0.4 on Hi4D. The failure stemmed not from its tracking head, but from cross-camera pose misalignment, causing human body surfaces to split and reconstruct inconsistently.

### Underperformance of Multi-View Trackers
MVTracker, designed specifically for multi-view setups, achieved a non-query accuracy $\delta_{\mathrm{N}}^{3D}$ of 20.8, barely matching the monocular TAPIP3D (20.6). In query view accuracy $\delta_{\mathrm{Q}}^{3D}$, TAPIP3D outperformed it (27.1 vs. MVTracker). Existing multi-view trackers fail to effectively exploit information from complementary views.

### Top Performance from Modular Trackers, Bottlenecked by Geometry
The highest overall performance was achieved by combining the monocular 3D tracker TAPIP3D with VGGT-$\Omega$ geometry (world accuracy $\delta_{\mathrm{W}}^{3D}=22.8$). However, replacing estimated geometry with ground-truth depth caused TAPIP3D accuracy to surge from 14.0 to 40.3 on DROID, and from 5.9 to 62.9 on Hi4D. This demonstrates that tracking progress is currently capped by imperfect geometry recovery rather than correspondence capabilities.

captions.F5: Qualitative comparison on Hi4D. Joint methods (SpatialTrackerV2, OmniX) exhibit severe 3D surface reconstruction errors (blue-to-red error scale in middle row), leading to divergent predicted trajectories (red lines indicating errors in bottom row). TAPIP3D paired with shared geometry yields the most stable results.

sections.heading: Conclusions and four key priorities for future research
sections.summary: TAPVid-MV highlights the true bottlenecks in dynamic multi-view point tracking. To achieve future breakthroughs, the authors propose strengthening dynamic geometry recovery, reporting decoupled geometry alongside tracking metrics, and solving contact-induced tracking drift.
sections.details:
This study underscores both the difficulties and opportunities of 3D point tracking across moving cameras. Based on the findings, the authors present four clear priorities for future work:

1. ### Dynamic Scene Geometry from Few Moving Cameras
Currently, no model reliably recovers depth and camera poses for dynamic scenes from a handful of moving cameras. Developing robust dynamic multi-view geometry foundation models is the single most critical prerequisite for 3D tracking.

2. ### Decoupled Evaluation of Geometry and Tracking
Future 3D tracking benchmarks must report underlying geometry reconstruction accuracy (depth and pose errors) on the same evaluation data. Otherwise, it is impossible to tell whether gains stem from superior tracking architectures or better geometric priors and training data.

3. ### Trackers that Truly Leverage Multi-View Information
Rather than merely tracking per view and combining results via geometry, models must actively exchange visual features across views in real time to resolve occlusions and ambiguities.

4. ### Resolving Identity Swapping and Long-Term Drift Under Contact
Even when provided with ground-truth geometry, trackers frequently suffer from ID swaps when objects or limbs interact, as well as surface drift over long horizons. These remain fundamental correspondence challenges.

To accelerate progress across the community, the authors have released the benchmark code, evaluation protocols, the Perpetua procedural generator, and 3D track annotations for 5,371 DROID episodes.

sections.heading: Appendix: DROID track generation pipeline and rigorous verification
sections.summary: For the DROID dataset, a specialized pipeline was developed to resolve specular reflections on the gripper and optimize wrist camera extrinsics. Across all datasets, automated filtering via 2D tracking consensus was paired with complete manual visual verification.
sections.details:
The appendix details the data curation pipelines ensuring benchmark fidelity.

### High-Precision Trajectory Generation on DROID
In DROID robot manipulation videos, specular reflections on metal grippers caused stereo depth holes, and wrist camera calibrations frequently drifted. To resolve depth artifacts, the authors performed "depth distillation" by taking the temporal median of depths within SAM masks while the gripper remained open at episode start. Furthermore, multi-camera extrinsics were optimized via differentiable registration combining CAD alignment against robot URDF models with Chamfer distance losses between point clouds.

### Rigorous Tracking Cleanup
Mesh fits on humans and objects frequently slip or detach at extremities such as hands and feet. In Harmony4D, forward-backward cycle-consistency consensus using TAPNext++ was applied to automatically discard mesh vertices conflicting with 2D image tracks. In PACE, handheld trinocular tracks collapsing toward camera centers or straying outside SAM masks were filtered out. Finally, human annotators inspected 3D projected tracks across all sequences, pruning invalid tracks to establish the final benchmark.

captions.F6: Detailed qualitative evaluations on DROID (top three rows) and PACE (bottom three rows). On DROID, joint methods confuse fast gripper motion with camera motion and depth, leading to catastrophic tracking failures at the end-effector.
captions.F8: Example of automated tracking cleanup in Harmony4D. Green points represent retained trajectories verified by image tracking consensus, while red points indicate rejected trajectories suffering from mesh misalignment or extreme limb deformation.

takeaways: Multi-view 3D point tracking with moving cameras remains unsolved by modern methods (including 4D foundation models), exhibiting near-zero accuracy in challenging domains like autonomous driving and close human contact.

The primary bottleneck in 3D point tracking lies in multi-view dynamic geometry recovery (depth and camera poses) rather than tracking algorithms, necessitating decoupled geometric reporting in future evaluations.
Existing multi-view trackers fail to effectively leverage complementary views, making modular pipelines ("strong geometry foundation model + monocular tracker") the most reliable approach at present.

Tracking failures during physical contact (identity swapping) and long-term surface drift persist even with perfect ground-truth geometry, highlighting core correspondence challenges that remain open.
limitations: Because real-world annotations rely on estimated depth, SLAM, and fitted meshes, evaluation at extremely tight metric thresholds (millimeter-level) may be influenced by residual annotation noise.
While rigid objects and articulated human bodies are represented, the benchmark does not cover highly non-rigid objects with high-degree local deformations, such as cloth or fluids.

Global alignment in the evaluation protocol relies on median distance scaling from the query point; comprehensive exploration of ranking sensitivity to alternative alignment methods remains future work.
